text: *Rajasaurus narmadensis* means "royal lizard of the [[@narmada|Narmada]]". It lived in western India about 67 million years ago, near the very end of the age of dinosaurs.

It was a [[theropod|theropod]], a two-legged meat-eater, about 8–9 metres long, as long as two cars parked end to end. On its head it had a rounded bump, like a small crown. Its closest relatives lived in [[@madagascar|Madagascar]] and South America. That's a clue that these lands were once joined.

spots: A bumpy horn above its eyes. It was probably for showing off to other Rajasaurus, like a peacock's tail.
Short, sharp, serrated teeth, like a steak knife. Rajasaurus was a meat-eater.
Its arms were very short, even shorter for its size than T. rex's. Its head did the hunting.
It walked on two powerful legs, built for striding.
A heavy tail balanced the big head, like a seesaw.
Its bones were dug up near Rahioli village in Gujarat in the 1980s and named in 2003.

quiz.prompt: Rajasaurus's closest relatives lived in Madagascar and South America. Why?

options.t: India, Madagascar and South America were once joined

quiz.reveal: Long ago, these lands were all part of a giant southern continent called Gondwana. As it broke apart, related animals ended up on different pieces. India and Madagascar stayed joined until about 88 million years ago.

sec.t:
In the early 1980s, a team from the Geological Survey of India, led by the [[geologist|geologist]] Suresh Srivastava, dug up bones near Rahioli village in Kheda district, Gujarat. The bones lay in rocks called the Lameta Formation, made of sand and mud laid down by rivers and lakes.

The bones waited in collections for years. Then Indian scientists, including Suresh Srivastava, Ashok Sahni and Ashu Khosla, studied them with the American scientists Jeffrey Wilson and Paul Sereno. They named the animal in 2003.

Scientific names follow fixed rules, as you can read in [[@dino-names|how dinosaurs get their names]]. The first part, *Rajasaurus*, joins the [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] and [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] word *raja*, king, with the Greek *sauros*, lizard. The second part, *narmadensis*, points to the Narmada river region, where many of India's dinosaur [[fossil|fossils]] have been found.

Only part of the skeleton was recovered: the skull roof with its crest, the braincase, parts of the backbone, hips, legs and tail. Scientists filled in the rest by comparing it with close relatives. That is why its length is an estimate.

Rajasaurus belonged to the abelisaurs, a family of big hunters that lived mainly on the southern continents. Abelisaurs had short, deep skulls, strong necks and [[@trex-arms|tiny arms]], even smaller for their size than those of T. rex. Rajasaurus's arms have not been found, but its relatives suggest they were very short.

They probably hunted big plant-eaters like the long-necked titanosaurs, whose [[@dino-eggs|eggs]] are found nearby in Kheda and Balasinor. The head did the hunting, grabbing and biting rather than reaching with the arms.

Abelisaurs lived in India, Madagascar, Africa and South America, lands that were once joined in [[gondwana|Gondwana]]. Rajasaurus's closest known cousin, Majungasaurus, lived in Madagascar at about the same time.

India had split from Madagascar about 88 million years ago and was drifting north as an island. Its animals carried their family links with them. [[@india-drift|India's long journey]] explains why.

When Rajasaurus lived, the [[@deccan|Deccan]] volcanoes were beginning some of the largest eruptions in Earth's history, spreading [[lava|lava]] over western and central India. In many places, the Lameta rocks that hold its bones lie just beneath these old lava layers. Not long afterwards, in Earth's terms, the [[asteroid|asteroid]] struck, and India's royal lizard vanished with the rest.

text: All three are frozen water falling from clouds, but they form in different ways. Snow is made of [[@earth-weird-frost-flowers|ice crystals]] that grow inside cold clouds and fall without melting. Hail is lumps of ice that grow inside thunderstorms, carried up and down by strong winds until they are too heavy to stay up.

Sleet means different things in different countries. In the USA, it means small ice pellets: [[@maths-snowflakes|snowflakes]] that melted on the way down and froze again before landing. In Britain and India, it usually means a slushy mix of rain and snow falling together.

sec.t:
High in a cloud, where it is well below freezing, water vapour turns straight into ice on tiny specks of dust. A crystal forms. More vapour freezes onto it, and it grows into a snowflake. Because of the way water [[molecule|molecules]] fit together, ice crystals have six sides, so almost every snowflake has [[@snowflake-six|six arms]].

If the air all the way to the ground stays cold, the flakes arrive as snow. Different [[@clouds-types|clouds]] and temperatures make different kinds of flakes. In India, that happens every winter in the high Himalaya, in places like Gulmarg in [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] and Auli in [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]]. In the USA, cities like Buffalo, near the [[@great-lakes|Great Lakes]], can get well over two metres of snow in a winter.

Wilson Bentley was a farmer in Jericho, Vermont. In 1885, at the age of 19, he became the first person known to photograph a single snowflake, using a camera attached to a [[microscope|microscope]]. Over his life, he photographed more than 5,000 of them. He found that each one had its own pattern, and his pictures helped make the idea that "no two snowflakes are alike" famous.

Sometimes snow falls through a layer of warmer air partway down, and melts into rain. If there is a cold layer close to the ground, the drops freeze again into small, hard pellets of ice. Americans call these ice pellets sleet. They bounce when they hit the ground.

If the cold layer near the ground is very thin, the raindrops don't have time to freeze in the air. They freeze the moment they touch something cold, like a road or a branch. That is freezing rain, and it can coat everything in a glassy layer of ice.

The biggest hailstone measured in the United States fell in Vivian, South Dakota, in 2010. It was about 20 cm across, about the size of a volleyball, and weighed close to 0.9 kg. The [[@weather-records|heaviest hailstone on record]] anywhere fell in Gopalganj, [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]], in 1986, and weighed about 1 kg.

Big hail can dent cars and break windows, so if hail starts falling, the best place is indoors, away from windows.

A snowflake is made of clear ice. A pile of snow looks white because light bounces around between all the tiny crystals and comes back out mixed together, all colours at once. Deep snow and [[glacier|glacier]] ice can look blue, because they soak up a little red light. Hail can look white or clear, depending on how much air was trapped as each layer froze.

text: Small space rocks hit Earth all the time. Most burn up high in the sky as shooting stars.

The bigger the rock, the rarer the hit. Pieces the size of a car arrive about once a year and usually explode harmlessly high up. Rocks big enough to flatten a city come perhaps once every few hundred or few thousand years. Ones big enough to threaten the whole planet, like the [[asteroid|asteroid]] that helped end the age of the dinosaurs, come only once in tens of millions of years.
Scientists watch the sky every night. They've found almost all the really big ones near Earth, and none is on course to hit us in the next 100 years.

quiz.prompt: In 2013 a space rock exploded high above Chelyabinsk in Russia, and about 1,500 people needed medical help. What hurt most of them?

quiz.reveal: The rock burst about 30 km up. Its shock wave arrived a minute or more after the flash and broke windows across the city. Many people had gone to their windows to look at the bright light, so flying glass caused most of the injuries.

sec.t:
Every day, about 100 tonnes of space material falls on Earth. Nearly all of it is dust, grains smaller than sand, that drifts down unnoticed. Slightly bigger bits make [[@shooting-stars|shooting stars]]. Every so often a rock survives the fall and lands as a [[@meteorites|meteorite]].

Bigger pieces tend to explode in the air before they reach the ground, because the pressure of rushing through the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] at tens of kilometres a second tears them apart. [[@satellites-help|Satellites]] spot several such airbursts every year, mostly over oceans and empty land.

On 30 June 1908, something exploded over a remote forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia. It flattened about 80 million trees over an area larger than the city of Delhi. No [[crater|crater]] was found, so it was probably a rock tens of metres wide that blew apart several kilometres up. Because almost nobody lived there, few people, if any, were killed.

On 15 February 2013, a rock about 20 m wide, as long as two school buses, streaked over the city of Chelyabinsk. It burst about 30 km up with a flash brighter than the Sun. The shock wave smashed windows across the city, and about 1,500 people were hurt, mostly by flying [[@glass-made|glass]]. It was a reminder that even fairly small rocks can do damage if they arrive over a city.

Since the 1990s, telescopes have systematically searched for near-Earth asteroids. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] have now found more than 9 out of 10 of those over 1 km wide, the size that could cause worldwide disaster. None of them is on a path to hit Earth for at least the next century.

Smaller asteroids, 140 m and up, could still devastate a region. Fewer than half of those are thought to have been found. New [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]] are joining the hunt, including the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began observing in 2025, and NASA's NEO Surveyor, a space telescope planned for launch in 2027.

sec.h: How scientists work out the risk

sec.t:
If a dangerous asteroid were found years in advance, it might be possible to nudge it off course. In 2022, NASA's [[@dart|DART]] mission crashed a spacecraft into a small asteroid moon and changed its [[orbit|orbit]], proving the idea can work.

The key is time. A gentle push decades ahead is far easier than a desperate one at the last minute. That is why astronomers keep searching every clear night, long before anything is on its way. And the big one, 66 million years ago, explained in [[@extinction|extinction]], remains the exception rather than the rule.

text: Flying is hard work. A bird must keep its body light, grow big flight muscles and burn a lot of food to stay in the air. When a bird can survive without flying, its body slowly changes over many generations, and the ability to fly can fade away.

That has happened again and again. Some birds grew too big and heavy to fly, like the ostrich and the emu. Some lived on islands with no hunters on the ground, like the dodo. And some, like penguins, [[@ocean-penguins-swim|swapped the sky for the sea]], turning their wings into flippers for "flying" underwater.

sec.t:
Ostriches, emus, rheas, cassowaries and kiwis belong to a group of birds called ratites. Their breastbones are flat, without the tall keel that anchors big flight muscles in [[@how-birds-fly|flying birds]]. A large male ostrich can weigh well over 100 kg, heavier than most grown-ups.

Instead of wings, they invested in legs. An ostrich can run at about 70 km/h and kick hard enough to scare off a lion. Emus in Australia can run at around 50 km/h. The cassowary of New Guinea and northern Australia has a dagger-like claw on each foot and is treated with great respect by people who live near it. For a big bird on open grassland, running fast and seeing far is a better plan than flapping.

Ostriches once lived in India too. Pieces of their eggshell, some carved into beads by [[@stone-age|Stone Age]] people, have been found at many sites across the country.

Penguins are the most extreme case. Their wings have become short, stiff flippers, and their bones are solid and heavy rather than hollow, which helps them dive. [[@wild-penguin-dads|Emperor penguins]] can reach more than 500 m below the surface.

Why not do both? A study of thick-billed murres, Arctic seabirds that fly and dive, gave a clue. Their wings are a compromise, and flying costs them more energy than almost any bird ever measured. Scientists think penguins' ancestors faced the same squeeze. Better swimming wings made flying harder, until flying was no longer worth it. In return, emperor penguins became superb divers in the [[@penguins-cold|freezing seas of Antarctica]].

Some birds sit in between. Chickens can flutter onto a wall but can't travel far. [[@galapagos|Galápagos cormorants]] have stubby wings and swim for their food. Even strong fliers can become flightless for a while. Ducks and geese shed all their main wing feathers at once each year. They stay grounded for a few weeks, often hiding on lakes, until new ones grow.

Some flightless giants are already gone. The [[@lost-moa|giant moa]] of New Zealand could stretch its head up to about 3.6 m, higher than a basketball hoop. It had no wings at all, and it died out within a few centuries of people arriving.

text: Koalas sleep so much because of what they eat. They live almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, full of fibre, low in nourishment and laced with chemicals that are poisonous to most animals.

Digesting them takes a lot of time and energy, and the leaves give back very little. So a koala saves energy the simplest way possible: by barely moving. It sleeps or sits still for about 18 to 22 hours a day, wedged into the fork of a tree.
That's not laziness. It is a clever way to live on a diet that would starve most other [[mammal|mammals]].

sec.t:
Eucalyptus trees grow all over Australia, and there are hundreds of kinds. Their leaves are full of oils and bitter chemicals that help protect them from being eaten. Few animals can live on them.

Koalas can. Their livers break down the poisons. Their teeth grind the leaves into a fine paste. And in their gut is a long pouch called a caecum, about 2 metres long, which is enormous for an animal about the size of a small dog. Inside it, trillions of [[microbe|microbes]] slowly break the leaves down.

Even so, a koala is fussy. It eats only certain kinds of eucalyptus and picks the youngest, most nutritious leaves. It can eat up to about 500 g of leaves a day.

Koalas have a slow metabolism, the rate at which the body burns fuel. Their brains are small for their body size, which also saves energy, since brains are greedy organs.

Koalas hardly need to drink. They get most of their water from leaves, though they do drink in hot weather and [[drought|droughts]]. On hot days, they hug the cool trunks of trees to stay comfortable.

So their day goes like this: sleep, eat a little, sleep, move to a new branch, eat some more, sleep. Most of their activity happens at night and around dusk.

{{story:fingerprints}}

Koalas have fingerprints with ridges, loops and swirls very like ours. Under a [[microscope|microscope]], they are hard to tell apart from human prints. Very few animals have them, mostly primates. Koalas [[evolve|evolved]] them separately, probably to help grip branches and handle leaves.

They also have a surprising voice. Male koalas give a deep bellow, a bit like a snoring roar, to show off to females and warn rivals. In 2013, scientists discovered why it is so deep: koalas have an extra pair of vocal folds, outside the voice box, that no other land mammal is known to have.

Koalas are [[marsupial|marsupials]], like kangaroos and [[@wild-wombat-cubes|wombats]]. A newborn koala is about the size of a jellybean. It crawls into its mother's pouch, which opens towards her back legs, and stays there for about six months, drinking milk.

Then comes a strange step. To digest eucalyptus, the joey needs the right microbes in its gut. So its mother makes a special soft poop called pap, and the joey eats it. After that, the joey can start on leaves. It rides on its mother's back until it is about a year old.

Koalas are not bears, despite the common name "koala bear". They are found only in Australia. Their numbers have fallen as forests are cleared for farms, roads and houses. Dogs and cars kill many, and a disease called chlamydia makes others ill.

The 2019 and 2020 [[@forest-fires|bushfires]] burned huge areas of koala forest. In 2022, the Australian government listed koalas as [[endangered|endangered]] in Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory.

Koalas are one of the slowest-living mammals around. Their only real rival for doing so little lives in the rainforests of South and Central America. The [[@power-sloth|sloth]] hangs upside down so still that algae grow on its fur.

text: A lever is a bar that turns on a point called a [[fulcrum|fulcrum]], like a seesaw.
Push far from the fulcrum and a small push can lift a heavy load close to it. You trade distance for force: your end moves a long way, while the heavy end moves only a little.
Scissors, bottle openers, hand pumps and your own arm are all levers.

myth: A lever gives you extra energy, letting you get something for nothing.
A lever only swaps force for distance. You push with less force, but you have to move your end much further. The total work you do stays the same, or a little more because of friction.

effort × its distance = load × its distance

sec.t:
Two children on a seesaw show the rule. If one child is twice as heavy, the lighter child must sit twice as far from the middle to balance. In maths, the push multiplied by its distance from the fulcrum must equal the load multiplied by its distance.

That's how a kid could, in theory, lift an elephant. A 4-tonne [[@elephants-talk|elephant]] sitting 1 m from the fulcrum would need a 30 kg child about 133 m away on the other side, roughly the width of a big cricket ground. The bar would have to be impossibly strong, but the maths works.

Levers come in three types, depending on where the fulcrum, the load and your push sit.

In the first kind, the fulcrum is in the middle, like a seesaw, scissors or a crowbar. In the second, the load is in the middle, like a wheelbarrow or a nutcracker. The wheel is the fulcrum, the load sits in the tray, and you lift the handles.

In the third kind, your push is in the middle. Tweezers, a [[@cricket-bat|cricket bat]] and a fishing rod work this way. These levers don't make lifting easier. Instead, they turn a small movement of your hand into a big, fast movement at the other end.

Your forearm is a third-kind lever. The elbow is the fulcrum, and your biceps [[@muscles|muscle]] pulls on the bone just below it. Because the muscle is attached so close to the joint, it must pull very hard, but a small shortening swings your hand a long way, quickly. That's useful for throwing.

Your jaw, your foot when you stand on tiptoe, and even your head nodding on your neck are levers too.

People have used levers for thousands of years. In ancient Egypt and [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], farmers lifted water with a *shaduf*: a long pole on a post, with a bucket at one end and a heavy weight at the other. Very similar well-sweeps are still seen in some villages in India and other countries.

Builders of the [[@pyramids|pyramids]] and of the brick cities of the [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley]] almost certainly used levers to shift heavy blocks, though we don't know all their methods. Levers often worked alongside ramps, rollers and later [[@pulleys|pulleys]].

Look around a kitchen and levers are everywhere: a tap handle, a bottle opener, tongs, the lid of a dustbin with a foot pedal. A car jack, a pair of pliers and the handle of a hand pump at a village well all trade a long, easy push for a short, strong one. Archimedes would recognise every one of them.

text: An old-style bulb has a very thin wire called a filament. Electricity pushes through it and heats it to about 2,500°C, until it glows white-hot. But most of the energy turns into heat, not light.

An LED, a *light-emitting diode*, works differently. Inside a tiny chip, [[@electricity-made|electricity]] makes [[electron|electrons]] jump down in energy, and each jump gives off a little burst of light. Very little heat is wasted.

sec.t:
Anything gets hot enough, and it glows. A stove coil turns dull red, and the [[@sun-what|Sun]], far hotter, shines white. Old bulbs used the same idea. The filament was coiled tightly so a long wire could fit inside, and the [[@glass-made|glass]] held no oxygen, so the wire couldn't burn up.

Most of what a hot filament gives off is invisible [[infrared|infrared]], which we feel as heat. Only about a tenth comes out as light your [[@eyes-colour|eyes]] can see.

Between old bulbs and LEDs came fluorescent tube lights, long familiar in Indian classrooms and offices. Electricity passes through a gas containing a little mercury, which gives off invisible [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light. A white powder coating the inside of the glass turns that ultraviolet into visible light. Tube lights and the curly CFL bulbs used far less power than filament bulbs, but their mercury makes them tricky to throw away safely.

In a fire station in Livermore, California, a hand-blown bulb has been glowing almost without a break since 1901. It's very dim and runs on low power, which helps it last. Firefighters and visitors watch it on a webcam, and it has outlived several of the cameras pointed at it.

Red and green LEDs were invented first. The first practical visible-light LED, a red one, was made in the USA in 1962. A bright blue LED took decades more, and you need blue to make white light. Three Japanese scientists won the 2014 Nobel Prize for it.

Most white LED bulbs today use a blue LED covered with a yellow coating. Some blue light shines through, the coating turns the rest yellow, and together they look white.

In 2015, the Government of India started the UJALA scheme to sell LED bulbs cheaply. More than 36 crore bulbs were handed out across the country. Because each LED uses so much less power than an old bulb, the scheme cut electricity use and bills in millions of homes.

LEDs also last many years. A good one can run for 25,000 hours or more, compared with about 1,000 for an old bulb. They now light streets, [[@made-phone-screens|phone screens]], traffic signals and cricket stadiums.

[[@fireflies|Fireflies]] make cold light too, with chemistry instead of electricity. Inside a firefly's tail, [[@how-glow-sticks|a chemical reaction makes light]] with almost no heat at all, a trick engineers took more than a century to match.

text: A projector does three jobs. It makes a very bright light. It shapes that light into a small picture. Then a [[@lenses-glasses|lens]] spreads the picture out so it lands, sharp and large, on a wall or screen far away.

The small picture might be a painted glass slide, a strip of film, a tiny screen or a chip full of moving mirrors. The idea has stayed the same for more than 350 years. Only the picture maker in the middle has changed.
Because the light spreads out as it travels, a projector placed farther back gives a bigger picture. A cinema projector at the back of a hall can fill a screen as wide as a cricket pitch is long.

st.reveal: The same amount of light now spreads over a picture twice as wide and twice as tall, so four times the area. Each patch of wall gets only a quarter of the light, which is why big pictures need very bright lamps.

sec.t:
The earliest projectors were called magic lanterns, and they were in use in Europe by the 1660s. Inside was a candle or oil lamp, a curved mirror behind it and a lens in front. Pictures were painted on glass slides and pushed through a slot.

Showmen travelled from town to town with them. They told ghost stories and fairy tales while images of skeletons, ships and kings glowed on a sheet. Some slides had moving parts, so a windmill could turn or a sailor could open his mouth.

Then came film. In 1895 the [[@hist-first-film|Lumière brothers]] showed short films in Paris with a machine that projected moving pictures. Only months later, in July 1896, the same films played at Watson's Hotel in Bombay. Within twenty years [[@dadasaheb-phalke|Dadasaheb Phalke]] was making Indian films for those projectors to show.

sec.h: Why the slide goes in upside down
sec.t:
A projector lens works a bit like your eye, but in reverse. Light from the top of the slide crosses over inside the lens and lands at the bottom of the screen. Light from the left ends up on the right.

So the picture comes out flipped both ways. That is why old slide projectors were loaded with every slide upside down and back to front. Film projectors had the same trick built in.

Focusing means sliding the lens forward or back until the crossed beams meet exactly at the screen. Too close or too far and each point of light smears into a blob, which is the blur you see when a teacher is still fiddling with the knob.

{{story:movies-move}}

Most projectors today make their picture electronically. One common kind uses a small see-through LCD screen with the light shining through it. Another kind, called DLP, uses a chip invented at Texas Instruments in 1987.

A DLP chip is covered in tiny mirrors, up to a few million of them, each smaller than the width of a hair. Every mirror is one [[@pixels|pixel]]. When a mirror tilts one way, it bounces light out through the lens and that dot on the screen glows. When it tilts the other way, the light is thrown into a dark corner and the dot goes dark.

The mirrors flick thousands of times a second. Your eye can't follow them, so it simply sees shades of grey. A spinning colour wheel or coloured lights add red, green and blue.

A projector can only add light, never take it away. On a bright afternoon the sun is already lighting the screen, so the projector's picture has to compete with it.

That is why cinemas are dark and why school projectors look faded with the curtains open. It is also why projectors have grown far brighter. Old ones used hot lamps that needed fans and burned out. Many newer ones use LEDs or [[@lasers|lasers]], which run cooler and last for years. Some are small enough to fit in a pocket and still cast a picture the size of a door.

text: Pablo Picasso (1881–1973) was a Spanish artist who spent most of his life in France. He is one of the most influential artists of the 1900s. Together with the French painter Georges Braque, he invented Cubism, a way of painting that breaks objects into flat, angular pieces and shows them from several sides at once.

Picasso never stuck with one style for long. Over about eighty years of work he painted, sculpted, made prints and pottery, and designed theatre costumes. His [[@famous-paintings|most famous painting]], *Guernica*, is a giant black, white and grey protest against the bombing of a town during the Spanish Civil War.

st.reveal: Picasso and Braque wanted to show more than a camera could. By combining different views in one picture, they showed what you would know about a face if you walked around it.

sec.t:
Picasso was born in Málaga, in the south of [[@spain|Spain]]. His father was an art teacher who gave him lessons from an early age. By his teens, Pablo could paint careful, realistic portraits and passed entrance exams for art schools in Barcelona and Madrid.

He soon grew bored with copying what the academies wanted. In 1904 he moved to [[@paris|Paris]], then the centre of the art world, where young artists from many countries were trying new ideas.

In 1907 Picasso painted *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon*, five women made of sharp, flat [[@shapes-angles|shapes and angles]], some with [[@art-masks-world|faces like masks]]. Even his friends were shocked. He had been looking at ancient Iberian [[@sculpture|sculpture]] and at African masks he saw in Paris museums.

Over the next few years he and Braque developed Cubism. Their paintings of guitars, bottles and people look as if they have been smashed and rebuilt. They also stuck real things onto their pictures, such as newspaper and wallpaper, inventing collage as a serious art form. These experiments opened the door to much of [[@modern-art|modern art]].

In April 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, German and Italian warplanes supporting General Franco bombed the Basque town of Guernica. Many civilians were killed. Picasso, living in Paris, was asked to paint a large [[mural|mural]] for the Spanish pavilion at the World's Fair that year.

He made *Guernica*: nearly 8 metres wide, painted only in black, white and grey, like a newspaper photograph. It shows a screaming horse, a bull, a mother holding her child and a broken soldier. There is no blood, yet the picture feels full of pain. It toured the world and became a symbol against war, especially as [[@world-war-two|the Second World War]] began two years later. Today it hangs in a museum in Madrid.

Picasso was hugely famous in his lifetime and kept working until he died at 91. He tried ceramics in his sixties, making thousands of plates, jugs and vases at a [[@pottery|pottery]] workshop in the south of France.

His personal life has been criticised. Several of the women close to him, some of whom were also artists, later described him as controlling and unkind. Today many museums mention this alongside his art. His influence is still everywhere, from Indian painters like M.F. Husain to cartoonists and designers who borrow his bold, broken shapes.

text: [[rhythm|Rhythm]] is the pattern of sounds and silences in time. To make a rhythm, you split time into equal beats, then group those beats and divide them into smaller pieces. That is counting, adding and making fractions, all in your ears and feet.

Every music tradition does this. A Hindustani tabla player counts a 16-beat cycle called teentaal. A Carnatic singer keeps an 8-beat cycle with hand claps and finger taps. A rock drummer counts "1, 2, 3, 4". The patterns repeat like times tables, and musicians play with them the way mathematicians play with numbers.

st.prompt: A rhythm can use short beats (1 count) and long beats (2 counts). How many different rhythms fill exactly 4 counts?
st.reveal: The five are 1+1+1+1, 2+1+1, 1+2+1, 1+1+2 and 2+2. For 5 counts there are 8, for 6 counts there are 13. Each answer is the sum of the two before it: the Fibonacci numbers.

d.try: Clap a pattern of 3 against 2. With your left hand, tap twice evenly while your right hand taps three times evenly in the same time. Say "pass the gol-den but-ter" to help. It feels tricky, but it is just the maths of fitting 3 and 2 into the same space, called a polyrhythm.
myth: Rhythm is pure feeling, and has nothing to do with maths.

Feeling matters, but rhythm is built on counting, fractions and repeating patterns. Indian musicians count talas on their fingers, and Western musicians divide each beat into halves, quarters and thirds.

sec.t:
Indian classical music is built on the *tala*, a cycle of beats that repeats again and again. In teentaal, the 16 beats are grouped 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. The first beat, called *sam*, is the "home". Musicians wander away into complicated patterns, and everyone waits to see them land back exactly on sam.

One favourite trick is the *tihai*: a phrase played three times so that its last note falls on sam. To make it land, the player has to calculate. If the phrase plus a gap is 5 beats long, three of them fill 15 beats, so it must start one beat after sam. Good [[@tabla|tabla]] players do this kind of maths at full speed, without stopping to think.

Sanskrit poetry has long and short [[syllable|syllables]]. A short syllable takes one count, a long one takes two. Poets wanted to know how many patterns could fill a line of a certain length.

Try it. For 1 count, there's one pattern. For 2 counts, two (short-short or long). For 3 counts, three. For 4 counts, five. Then 8, 13, 21. Each number is the sum of the two before it. The scholar Virahanka described this, sometime around 600 to 800 CE. Gopala and Hemachandra wrote about it later. The Italian mathematician Fibonacci wrote about the same numbers in 1202, which is how they got his name. These numbers also turn up in pine cones and sunflowers, as the story of [[@fibonacci-nature|Fibonacci in nature]] shows.

Even earlier, the scholar Pingala listed rhythm patterns with a method that works like counting in [[@binary-code|binary]], with short and long standing in for 0 and 1.

{{story:fibonacci-nature}}

In Western music, a note can last a whole beat, half a beat or a quarter of a beat. That's [[@fractions|fractions]]. A "time signature" at the start of a piece, like 3/4, tells players there are three beats in a bar, each a quarter note. A waltz goes ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three. Most pop songs are in 4/4.

Some music uses odd numbers. Folk music from the Balkans often has 7 or 11 beats, grouped as 2 + 2 + 3 or similar. Carnatic music has talas of 5, 7 and 9 beats too.

In 2005, the computer scientist Godfried Toussaint noticed something surprising. Take a number of beats, like 8, and try to spread 3 strong beats among them as evenly as possible. You get a pattern of 3 + 3 + 2. That is the Cuban tresillo, found in rhythms all over the world. Many famous rhythms turn out to follow the same simple maths rule, one also used inside computers.

Your body keeps rhythms too. Your heart beats about 70 to 100 times a minute at rest in children. You breathe and walk in steady patterns. When a song's beat matches your walking pace, around 100 to 120 beats a minute, you naturally want to tap along.

Doctors listen to the rhythm of the heart for clues about health. Run up a flight of stairs and that drumbeat in your chest speeds up at once, for a reason explained in the story of [[@heartbeat-exercise|your heartbeat]].

text: Negative numbers are numbers less than zero, like −1, −5 or −273. Nobody invented them in one moment. Chinese mathematicians were using them about 2,000 years ago to solve problems about trade and money. In 628 CE, the Indian mathematician [[@brahmagupta|Brahmagupta]] wrote the first full set of rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing them.

Europeans took much longer to accept them. Many thought it made no sense to have less than nothing. Today you meet negative numbers on [[@thermometer|thermometers]], bank statements and in lifts that go below the ground floor.

st.reveal: Red rods were positive and black rods were negative. Today accountants say a business that is losing money is "in the red", the reverse of the ancient Chinese system.

sec.t:
In [[@ancient-china|ancient China]], people calculated by laying small [[@bamboo|bamboo]] or bone rods on a board. A famous book called The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, put together about 2,000 years ago, used red rods for positive amounts and black ones for negative amounts.

This let people solve problems with several unknowns, such as working out the price of different grains from a few market sales. The book gave rules for adding and subtracting the coloured rods, so negative amounts could appear partway through a sum and then cancel out.

Indian and Arab mathematics reached Europe slowly. Even in the 1500s, the German mathematician Michael Stifel called negative numbers absurd. Others called them false or fictitious. If a problem gave a negative answer, they often said it had no answer.

Gradually, bankers and merchants found negatives useful for debts. Scientists needed them for temperatures and positions. By the 1700s most mathematicians accepted them as ordinary numbers. Number lines, with negatives stretching left of zero, became common in schoolbooks much later.

[[@maths-sport|Sport is full of them too]]. In golf, a player who takes fewer shots than expected has a score like −3, and the lowest score wins. In football league tables, a team that has let in more goals than it scored has a negative goal difference. Cricket's net run rate, used to split teams level on points in [[tournament|tournaments]], can also dip below zero.

Negative numbers are everywhere once you look. In winter, the temperature in Leh, in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], can drop below −20 °C. Water freezes at 0 °C, which is 32 °F, so a Delhi morning at 5 °C feels very different from one at −5 °C. Different [[@temperature-scales|temperature scales]] put zero in different places. The coldest temperature possible, called absolute zero, is −273.15 °C.

Lifts use negatives too. In some buildings a button marked −1 or B1 takes you below the ground floor, and [[@elevators|elevators]] in deep metro stations go further still. The shore of the [[@dead-sea|Dead Sea]], between Jordan and Israel, is more than 430 metres [[@extreme-lowest-point|below sea level]], the lowest dry land on Earth. The salty water there makes swimmers float, as you can read in [[@lakes-salty|salty lakes]]. In the United States, Badwater Basin in Death Valley sits about 86 metres (282 feet) below sea level.

text: Mallakhamb is a sport from India in which athletes do gymnastics and yoga-like poses on a wooden pole or a hanging rope. They climb, twist, hang upside down, lock their legs around the pole and hold impossible-looking shapes, all in a few breathless minutes.

The pole is about 2.6 m tall, smooth and polished, and thicker at the bottom than the top. Athletes rub castor oil and dust their hands so they can grip and slide. The sport is strongest in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, and in 2013 Madhya Pradesh made it its official state sport. Strength, balance and courage come together in it, much like [[@gymnastics|gymnastics]] without the springboard.

sec.t:
The name says it all. *Malla* means wrestler and *khamb* means pole. Wrestlers once practised grips and throws on a wooden post, which never got tired and never complained. Over time, the training became a sport of its own.

It is mentioned in the *Manasollasa*, a Sanskrit book about royal life written in 1135 CE by King Somesvara III of the Chalukya [[dynasty|dynasty]]. The modern form is credited to Balambhatt Dadadeodhar, who was a fitness teacher for the court of the Peshwa Bajirao II in Pune in the early 1800s. Even today, it shares a home with [[@wrestling-india|Indian wrestling]] in many akharas.

There are three main kinds. Pole mallakhamb uses the fixed wooden pole. Rope mallakhamb uses a thick cotton rope hanging from above. Athletes wrap it around their arms and legs and climb into poses, without using knots. Rope mallakhamb became especially popular with girls.

Hanging mallakhamb is a shorter pole that hangs from hooks and chains, so it swings while the athlete moves. That makes balance even harder.

Many poses come from yoga and are given names such as the peacock or the bow. The mix of strength and stretch is close to what researchers study in [[@yoga-science|yoga science]].

{{story:gymnastics}}

In 1936, a club from Amravati, Maharashtra, travelled to the Berlin Olympics and showed Indian sports, including mallakhamb and [[@sport-kho-kho-world|kho-kho]]. European spectators had never seen anything like it.

For decades after, mallakhamb remained mostly a school and club sport in India. National championships began in 1962, and the Mallakhamb Federation of India organises competitions today.

Mallakhamb has had a big comeback. Teams performed on TV talent shows, and short videos of children on the rope spread on social media. In 2019, Mumbai hosted the first Mallakhamb World Championship, with athletes from countries including the United States, Germany, Japan and Malaysia.

Some players never thought of themselves as athletes. In Bastar, Chhattisgarh, a group of village children trained in mallakhamb became famous for their performances and won national medals.

Watch closely and you can see clever physics. Athletes keep their weight close to the pole, so they need less strength. When they stick their legs out sideways, the pole works like a [[@lever-lift|lever]], and the farther out the legs go, the harder the muscles must work.

Coaches train beginners, children and adults alike, to build core strength first, because the belly and back muscles hold every pose together. It is also why many Indian martial arts, like [[@sport-kalaripayattu|kalaripayattu]], start with similar body training.

text: Motivation is the push that gets you to do something. It comes from your brain's reward system, a set of connected areas deep in the brain that predict which actions will pay off. When your brain expects something good, it releases a chemical called [[dopamine|dopamine]], and you feel the pull to go and get it.

Psychologists split motivation into two kinds. Intrinsic motivation comes from inside: you play football because it's fun. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside: you tidy your room because you'll get pocket money. Both are real, and most of what we do mixes the two. A cricketer may play for the joy of hitting a clean cover drive and also for a place in the team.
Motivation fades when the brain stops expecting a reward, or when the reward feels too far away.

st.reveal: In the 1973 Stanford study, children who had expected a reward later spent less free time drawing. The reward may have turned drawing from play into a job. Later studies found surprise rewards and praise for effort did less harm.

myth: Dopamine is the brain's pleasure chemical.

Research suggests dopamine is mostly about wanting, expecting and chasing rewards, and about learning what's worth doing. The good feeling of actually enjoying something seems to involve other brain chemicals as well.
facts: intrinsic (from inside) and extrinsic (from outside rewards)

sec.h: Wanting is not the same as liking
sec.t:
For years, people called dopamine the pleasure chemical. Then, in the 1990s, researchers at the University of Michigan found something odd. Rats whose dopamine was blocked still made happy faces when they tasted sugar. They just wouldn't make any effort to get it.

So dopamine seems to be about wanting, not liking. It rises when you spot a chance of a reward, which is why the moment before opening a present can feel more exciting than the present itself. [[@video-games|Video games]] use this cleverly, with surprise prizes and levels that are always almost finished.

Two American psychologists, Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, spent decades studying what makes motivation last. They concluded people need three things. They need some choice in what they do. They need to feel they're getting better at it. And they need to feel connected to other people.

Athletes often describe this. The javelin thrower [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]], who won India's first Olympic gold in athletics in 2021, began training as a teenager to get fitter. He kept going for years because he loved getting better. Coaches in [[@sports-science|sports science]] now talk about small, clear goals that let athletes feel progress every week.

Motivation isn't a fixed amount you either have or don't. It drops when you're tired, hungry or stressed, and when a goal seems impossibly far off. Breaking a big task into small steps gives the brain more chances to feel it's winning. Ticking off a list, or colouring in a chart, turns invisible progress into something the brain can see.

Waiting to feel motivated before starting doesn't always work, either. Often starting comes first, and the motivation follows once your brain sees some progress. Over time, things you do regularly can become [[@habits|habits]], which need much less motivation at all.

text: Railways came to India in the 1850s, built by British companies while the East India Company ruled much of the country. On 16 April 1853, a train of 14 carriages carrying about 400 guests left Bori Bunder in Bombay for Thane, about 34 km away. It was pulled by three [[@steam-engine|steam engines]] named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan. The trip took about an hour and a quarter.

Within fifty years, lines linked most big cities. After independence in 1947, the railways became Indian Railways, run by the government. It now has about 68,000 km of routes, more than 7,000 stations and around 12 lakh staff, and it carries close to 2 crore passenger journeys on a typical day.

st.reveal: The United States has the longest network, though most of it carries freight rather than passengers. China and Russia come next, and India is fourth. India's trains do carry far more passengers than America's, though.

sec.t:
The railways were built mainly to serve British interests. Trains could carry raw cotton, tea, coal and grain from inland India to [[@sea-ports|ports like Bombay and Calcutta]], to be shipped to Britain. They also let the army move soldiers quickly. After the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]], the British pushed railway building even faster.

Companies building the lines were promised a guaranteed profit, paid from Indian taxes if needed. Much of the steel and many engines came from Britain. Indian workers did most of the hard digging and building, cutting through hills and bridging huge rivers like the Ganga, often in dangerous conditions.

Even so, Indians soon made the railways their own. Trains let pilgrims reach faraway temples, families visit relatives and workers travel to cities for jobs. People from different regions and castes shared crowded carriages. Leaders of the freedom movement, including [[@gandhi|Gandhi]], travelled the country by third-class train to meet ordinary people.

Trains also carried sorrow. During [[@partition|Partition]] in 1947, millions crossed the new borders, many of them packed into trains, and some of those journeys ended in terrible violence.

Some of India's railways climb mountains. [[@india-wonder-toy-train|The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway]], opened in 1881, winds up to over 2,000 metres in loops and zigzags. The Nilgiri Mountain Railway climbs to Ooty, and the Kalka–Shimla line passes through more than a hundred [[@tunnels|tunnels]]. Together they are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. So is Mumbai's Chhatrapati [[@shivaji|Shivaji]] Maharaj Terminus, a grand Victorian Gothic station finished in 1888.

Indian Railways keeps changing. Most lines have been converted to one wide track gauge and electrified. [[@vande-bharat|Vande Bharat trains]], designed and built in India, began running in 2019. [[@india-wonder-chenab-bridge|The Chenab Bridge]], opened in 2025, carries trains about 359 metres above a river in [[@kashmir|Jammu and Kashmir]]. A high-speed line between Mumbai and [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]], using Japanese [[@bullet-trains|bullet train]] technology, is being built.

The United States has a longer network, mostly for freight. But few countries depend on their trains the way India does.

text: Scratch and Python are both programming languages, ways of giving instructions to a computer. Scratch is made for beginners, especially children. Instead of typing, you drag colourful blocks that say things like "move 10 steps" or "repeat 4 times" and snap them together to make games, animations and stories.

Python is a typed language, but it was designed to be easy to read. It is used by beginners and by professionals at big companies, space agencies and universities. Many people start with Scratch and move on to Python, because the big ideas are the same.

st.prompt: In Scratch, you can't snap two blocks together if they don't make sense. Why did the designers do this?

options.t: So beginners can't make typing or grammar mistakes
To make the programs run faster
Because the computer has no keyboard

st.reveal: In typed languages, a missing bracket or a spelling slip can stop a whole program. Scratch blocks only fit together in ways that work, like puzzle pieces. That lets beginners focus on ideas instead of punctuation.

myth: Python got its name from the snake.
Its creator, Guido van Rossum, named it after Monty Python's Flying Circus, a British comedy show he enjoyed. The snake logo came later.
facts: from the comedy show Monty Python's Flying Circus

sec.t:
Scratch was created at the MIT Media Lab in the USA by a team led by Mitchel Resnick, and launched for free in 2007. Its mascot is an orange cartoon cat. You choose characters, called sprites, and give them instructions by stacking blocks. Click the green flag and the program runs. If the cat walks off the screen, you can see the mistake straight away and fix it.

The blocks are shaped like puzzle pieces. A block that needs a number has a round hole for it. A block that asks a yes-or-no question has pointed ends. Blocks only fit together in ways that make sense, so you can't make the kind of typing mistakes that trip up beginners in other languages.

sec.h: Python: code that reads like English
sec.t:
Python was created by a Dutch programmer named Guido van Rossum. He began it as a hobby over the Christmas break in 1989 and released it in 1991. He named it after *Monty Python's Flying Circus*, a British comedy show, because he wanted the name to be short, unusual and a little silly.

Python is famous for being tidy. Spaces at the start of each line show which instructions belong together, so a Python program is laid out a bit like a well-organised list. Making a computer say hello takes just one line of code.

Python is used for an enormous range of jobs, partly because volunteers have written thousands of free add-ons for it, called libraries. Scientists use it to analyse data from telescopes and [[gene|gene]] studies. Websites use it behind the scenes. It is one of the main languages used to build [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] systems, and NASA engineers have used it to process data and run tests. In 2025, Python topped several popularity rankings of programming languages.

It is also widely taught in schools in India, the USA and elsewhere, because students can do real things with it quickly, from drawing shapes to building simple games.

Underneath, Scratch and Python teach the same thinking. You break a big problem into small steps, which is what an [[@algorithms|algorithm]] is. You repeat actions using loops. You make decisions with "if this, then that". You store information in variables, like a score in a game.

That is why moving from Scratch to Python feels less like starting over and more like swapping a bicycle with training wheels for a proper bike. And once you know Python, learning other [[@coding-languages|coding languages]] becomes much easier.

text: The Indian National Army, or INA, was an army of Indians formed during the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] to fight British rule. Most of its soldiers had been in the British Indian Army and were captured by Japan in Southeast Asia. Others were Indian workers and traders living in Malaya, Burma and Singapore.

From 1943 it was led by [[@subhas-bose|Subhas Chandra Bose]], known as Netaji. Fighting beside Japanese forces, the INA tried to push into India through Manipur and Nagaland in 1944. It was defeated. Yet after the war, when the British put its officers on trial, the INA became a symbol of courage for millions of Indians.

st.prompt: In 1945 the British put three INA officers, a Hindu, a Muslim and a Sikh, on trial at the Red Fort. What happened?

options.t: Protests spread across India and their sentences were cancelled
They were quietly found guilty and forgotten

st.reveal: The officers were found guilty of waging war against the King. But huge protests and strikes across India pushed the British army chief to cancel their punishment. The trials made the INA famous at home.

n.certNote: Historians agree on the main events. They disagree about how much the INA helped end British rule, and about its alliance with Japan during the war.

sec.t:
In February 1942, Japan captured [[@singapore|Singapore]], then a British base. Tens of thousands of Indian soldiers became prisoners. A captain named Mohan Singh persuaded many of them to form an army to free India, with Japanese support.

The first INA broke up within the year, because its leaders did not trust Japan's aims. It came back to life in 1943, when Subhas Bose arrived in Southeast Asia after a long, secret journey by submarine from Germany. He had left India in disguise in 1941, escaping house arrest.

In 1944, INA units joined a Japanese attack on Imphal and Kohima in northeast India. They raised their flag at Moirang in Manipur. But the attack failed. British and Indian troops held their ground, supplies ran out, the [[monsoon|monsoon]] turned paths to mud, and many soldiers died of hunger and disease.

By 1945 the INA was retreating through Burma. Japan surrendered in August. Bose was reported to have died after a plane crash in Taiwan that month. Some people in India refused to believe it, and the question was debated for decades.

After independence, INA soldiers were not taken back into the Indian Army, but the government later recognised them as freedom fighters. Lakshmi Sahgal returned to medicine and ran a clinic in Kanpur for decades. In 2002, aged 87, she stood for election as President of India.

sec.h: The trials that shook the Raj
sec.t:
In late 1945 the British put three INA officers on trial at Delhi's [[@red-fort|Red Fort]]: Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon. One was Muslim, one Hindu and one Sikh, so people of every community felt the trial was about them. Lawyers including Jawaharlal Nehru and Bhulabhai Desai defended them.

The three were found guilty, but protests were so strong that their punishments were cancelled. In early 1946, sailors of the Royal Indian Navy also rose up. Some historians think these events showed Britain it could no longer rely on Indian soldiers to hold India. Others argue that the bigger reasons were the war's cost and the long freedom struggle. Many also criticise the INA's alliance with Japan, whose army treated prisoners and civilians very harshly. The debate about the INA's place in the story of 1947 is still alive.

text: Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist minister who became the best-known leader of the American [[@civil-rights|civil rights movement]]. He fought to end laws that kept Black and white Americans apart and to win equal rights, including the right to vote.

King believed in non-violence, which he learned partly from [[@gandhi|Gandhi]]. He led boycotts and marches, went to jail many times, and gave speeches that moved millions. He was killed in 1968, aged 39. Today the third Monday of January is Martin Luther King Jr. Day, a national holiday in the USA.

st.prompt: King's most famous words, "I have a dream", come from a speech in 1963. Were they in the speech he had written down?

options.t: No, he spoke that part without notes

st.reveal: The "dream" section was not in his prepared text, though he had used similar words before. Witnesses say gospel singer Mahalia Jackson called out to him to tell the crowd about the dream, and he set his notes aside.

d.try: King's "I Have a Dream" speech repeats one phrase again and again to build power. Write a short speech about a change you'd like to see at school, using a repeated opening such as "I hope". Read it aloud to someone and notice how the repetition sounds.
myth: King was popular with most Americans during his lifetime.
In polls in the 1960s, many Americans disapproved of him, and the FBI secretly watched him for years. His reputation grew after his death, and his birthday became a national holiday in 1986.

sec.t:
King was born in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1929. His father and grandfather were both preachers at the same church. As a child he saw segregation close up. A white friend's parents told him they could no longer play together once school started, because the schools were separate.

He was a quick student and skipped two grades, entering Morehouse College at 15. He later earned a doctorate at Boston University and became a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1954.

In December 1955, [[@rosa-parks|Rosa Parks]] was arrested in Montgomery for refusing to give up her bus seat. Local leaders organised a boycott of the city's buses and chose the 26-year-old King to lead it. His house was bombed during the boycott, though his family was unhurt. He urged his supporters not to answer violence with violence.

After 381 days, the courts ended segregation on Montgomery's buses, and King became known across the country.

In 1959, King and his wife Coretta spent about a month in India. They met Prime Minister [[@nehru|Nehru]] and visited places linked with Gandhi. On arriving he said, "To other countries I may go as a tourist, but to India I come as a pilgrim."

He came home even more committed to non-violent protest, which he saw as a way to change laws and also change hearts. He later wrote that India had convinced him that non-violent resistance was the most powerful weapon available to oppressed people.

In 1963, King was jailed in Birmingham, Alabama, during protests. In his cell he wrote a long letter, on scraps of newspaper at first, explaining why people could not wait patiently for justice. His "Letter from Birmingham Jail" is still studied in schools.

That August, about 2.5 lakh people joined the March on Washington. He stood on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, built to honour [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]]. There he spoke of his dream that his four children would one day "not be judged by the colour of their skin but by the content of their character."

In 1964 King won the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]], the youngest winner up to then. He gave the prize money to the movement.

{{story:nobel-peace}}

Laws protecting civil rights and voting passed in 1964 and 1965.

King then spoke out about poverty and against the [[@vietnam|Vietnam War]], which cost him support. On 4 April 1968 he was shot in Memphis, Tennessee, where he had gone to support striking rubbish collectors.

Like other famous people, he had faults. Researchers later found that parts of his doctoral thesis copied other writers without credit. His achievements, though, are not in doubt.

A memorial to him opened in [[@washington-dc|Washington, D.C.]] in 2011, near the Lincoln Memorial. It shows him carved from a huge block of [[granite|granite]].

text: The samurai were Japan's warrior class. They first rose to power in the 12th century and remained an elite group until the 1870s.

At first, samurai were armed servants of noble families and fought mainly as mounted archers. In 1185, after a long war between two great clans, Minamoto no Yoritomo set up a military government led by a shogun, a supreme general. Emperors stayed on the throne, but for nearly 700 years shoguns and samurai held the real power. Samurai served lords called daimyo and were expected to be loyal, brave and disciplined. In peaceful times they became officials, teachers and scholars. In the 1870s, Japan's new government abolished their special status.

st.reveal: Portuguese traders blown off course reached the island of Tanegashima carrying matchlock guns. Japanese smiths quickly copied them. Within a few decades, thousands of guns were used in battle, and samurai armies changed how they fought.

myth: Samurai always fought with swords, in honourable one-on-one duels.
Early samurai fought mainly with bows from horseback, and later armies used spears and guns in large formations. Battles could be just as messy and tricky as anywhere else.
facts: bows, then swords, spears and guns

sec.h: The way of the bow and horse
sec.t:
Early samurai prized archery above all. Their long bows were taller than a person, made of [[@bamboo|bamboo]] and wood glued in layers. A warrior was expected to shoot while riding at full gallop.

Their armour was made of small lacquered plates laced together with silk cords, colourful and flexible. Swords were weapons for close fighting. The famous curved katana, made from carefully folded and hardened steel, became the symbol of the samurai later, and craftsmen still forge them today.

In the 1500s, Japan broke into a long civil war, with lords fighting each other. In 1543, Portuguese sailors landed on the island of Tanegashima with matchlock guns. Japanese smiths copied them quickly.

At the Battle of Nagashino in 1575, the warlord Oda Nobunaga's gunners fired in turns from behind wooden fences and cut down a charging cavalry army. Lords built tall castles with white plaster walls and stone bases. The most famous is Himeji Castle, now a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site, nicknamed the White Heron for its graceful shape. Japan's castles had a lot in common with the [[@knights-castles|castles of Europe]], though they looked very different.

sec.h: Warriors in a time of peace
sec.t:
In 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun and brought the wars to an end. His family ruled for over 250 years from Edo, the city now called [[@tokyo|Tokyo]].

Samurai still wore two swords as a mark of rank, but few ever fought a battle. They worked as government officials, ran schools and wrote books. The poet Matsuo Basho, master of the [[@haiku|haiku]], was born into a samurai family. Many samurai practised Zen meditation, part of a Buddhist tradition that reached Japan from India by way of China.

In 1853, American warships arrived and forced Japan to open its ports. Japan then modernised fast. In 1868, power returned to the emperor.

The new government built a modern army of ordinary conscripts and abolished the special status of samurai. In 1876, wearing swords in public was banned. Some samurai rebelled, but they were defeated. The idea of a samurai code called *bushido* became famous worldwide around 1900, largely through a book in English by Nitobe Inazo, long after the samurai themselves had gone.

text: The [[@forbidden-city|Forbidden City]] is the old imperial palace in the middle of Beijing, the capital of China. It was built between 1406 and 1420 for the Yongle Emperor of the Ming [[dynasty|dynasty]]. It was home to 24 emperors, their families and thousands of servants until the last emperor gave up the throne in 1912.

It was called "forbidden" because no one could enter or leave without the emperor's permission. Behind a moat and walls about 10 metres high, it covers about 72 hectares, roughly the size of 100 football fields, with around 980 buildings. Since 1925 it has been the Palace Museum, and it is now one of the most visited [[@museums|museums]] in the world.

st.prompt: Which colour of roof tile was meant for the emperor's buildings in the Forbidden City?
st.reveal: Yellow was the colour of the emperor, linked to the centre and the earth in Chinese tradition. Almost all the main halls have glazed yellow roofs. A few buildings, such as the library and the princes' quarters, have black or green tiles instead.

d.try: Draw a palace on squared paper. Draw one straight line down the middle from top to bottom, then put the most important room on that line and make the left and right halves mirror images. You have just used the same idea as the Forbidden City's builders.
myth: The Forbidden City has exactly 9,999 and a half rooms.
This is a popular legend, linked to the idea that only heaven could have 10,000 rooms. Surveys count far fewer, around 8,700 room spaces in about 980 buildings.
facts: 1406–1420, under the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty
about 72 hectares, behind a moat and 10 m walls

sec.t:
The whole palace is laid out along a straight north–south line. The most important halls stand on that line, one behind another, and the buildings on the left and right mirror each other. This [[@symmetry|symmetry]] was meant to show order and harmony, with the emperor at the centre of everything.

Visitors entered from the south through the Meridian Gate. Beyond it lie three great halls on raised marble terraces. The biggest is the Hall of Supreme Harmony, where emperors held major ceremonies on a golden throne. The private living quarters lay further north, and at the very back is an imperial garden of rocks, old trees and pavilions.

Almost nothing in the palace is decorated by accident. Yellow roof tiles were reserved for the emperor. Dragons, the symbol of the emperor, appear on roofs, walls, thrones and robes. Nine was an imperial number, so the big doors have rows of nine golden knobs, nine across and nine down.

Along the corners of each roof sits a parade of small animal figures. The more figures, the more important the building. The Hall of Supreme Harmony is the only one with ten.

sec.h: The emperor who sent the treasure fleet
sec.t:
The Yongle Emperor, who built the palace, also sent the admiral [[@zheng-he|Zheng He]] on giant voyages across the Indian Ocean. His fleets visited Calicut in Kerala and sailed as far as East Africa, bringing back gifts that included a giraffe.

When the last emperor, Puyi, gave up the throne in 1912, China became a [[republic|republic]]. He was allowed to stay inside the palace for a few more years, until 1924. The palace then opened as a museum, and today its collection holds more than 1.8 million objects, from bronzes and paintings to clocks given to emperors by European visitors. Many of the finest treasures were shipped away during China's civil war, and they are now in the National Palace Museum in Taipei. A short drive north of the city, crowds now walk the [[@great-wall|Great Wall]], another reminder of how China's rulers once guarded their land.

text: Mongolia is a large, landlocked country between Russia and China, mostly made of high grassland, mountains and the Gobi Desert. It is about half the size of India, but only about 35 lakh people live there, which makes it the most thinly populated country in the world.

Roughly a quarter of Mongolians are herders who live as nomads, or partly as nomads. They don't wander at random. Each family moves its animals between a few known camps through the year, following grass and water: a sheltered valley in winter, open pasture by a river in summer. They live in round felt tents called [[@life-homes-world|gers]], which they take with them. In winter, temperatures can fall below minus 40°C.

st.reveal: A ger has a folding lattice wall, roof poles, a central crown and layers of felt and canvas. A family that has done it all their lives can put it up in an hour or two and take it down even faster.

sec.t:
A ger has a folding wooden lattice wall, long roof poles and a round wooden crown at the top that lets out smoke and lets in light. Thick layers of sheep's-wool felt keep out the cold, and a white canvas cover goes over the top. A stove in the middle burns wood or dried dung for cooking and heat.

The door always faces south, away from cold north winds. Inside, there are customs about where to sit: guests go to the left, the place of honour is at the back, opposite the door. A family can put up a ger in an hour or two. Many families in Ulaanbaatar still live in gers on the edges of the city. In winter, smoke from thousands of their coal stoves makes the capital's air some of the dirtiest in the world.

Mongolian herders talk about the "five snouts": [[@horses|horses]], camels, cattle (including yaks), sheep and goats. In a recent count there were about 65 million animals, roughly 20 for every person.

Each animal has its job. Sheep give wool for felt, and meat. Goats give cashmere, the soft hair spun into expensive sweaters. Two-humped Bactrian [[@camels|camels]] carry loads across the Gobi. Mares are milked in summer, and the milk is [[@fermentation|fermented]] into a fizzy, slightly sour drink called airag.

The hardest times are a dzud, a winter so harsh, or following a summer so dry, that animals starve or freeze. In bad dzud years, millions of animals have died, and some families have had to give up herding and move to the city.

{{story:genghis-khan}}

Mongolians have a saying that a [[@mongols|Mongol]] without a horse is like a bird without wings. Children learn to ride very young. In the summer festival of Naadam, the "three manly games" are wrestling, horse racing and [[@archery|archery]]. Women and girls take part in archery and racing too. The jockeys in the horse races are often children, riding across the open steppe for many kilometres.

Some eight hundred years ago, horsemen like these followed [[@genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]], who united the Mongol tribes in 1206. His [[descendant|descendants]] built the largest connected land [[empire|empire]] in history.

The Gobi is one of the richest places in the world for [[@dino-museums|dinosaur fossils]]. In 1923, an American [[expedition|expedition]] led by Roy Chapman Andrews found nests of [[fossil|fossil]] [[@dino-eggs|dinosaur eggs]]. The place became known as the Flaming Cliffs, for the way its red rocks glow at sunset. The same expedition found the first known skull of [[@velociraptor-real|Velociraptor]] there. Fossil hunters still find bones in the Gobi, sometimes simply lying on the surface after a windstorm.

text: India has so many scripts because one ancient script, Brahmi, spread across a huge area over more than 2,000 years, and each region slowly shaped it in its own way. Different writing materials, different languages and different royal courts pulled the letters in different directions. It's a bit like one family whose children's [[@words-handwriting|handwriting]] drifted further apart with every generation.

Today India uses more than a dozen major scripts, including Devanagari, Bengali, [[@punjabi-gurmukhi|Gurmukhi]], Gujarati, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. Urdu and Kashmiri use a [[@arabic-script|Perso-Arabic script]], and Santali has its own script, Ol Chiki, created in 1925.

st.prompt: Many south Indian scripts, like Malayalam and Telugu, are round and curly. What is one popular explanation?

options.t: Straight lines would split the palm leaves people wrote on
Letters were carved in soft stone that cracked at corners

st.reveal: For centuries, people in the south scratched letters onto dried palm leaves with a metal stylus. Long straight lines along the leaf could split it along its veins, so curves were safer. It's a popular explanation, and probably one reason among several.

n.certNote: How scripts changed from Brahmi is well studied. Where Brahmi itself came from, and what the older Indus script says, are still debated.

sec.t:
The oldest readable Indian script is Brahmi, carved on rocks and pillars by Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] in the 3rd century BCE. Over the next thousand years, it split into northern and southern branches. The northern branch led, through scripts such as Siddham, Sharada and Nagari, to Devanagari, Bengali and Gurmukhi. The southern branch led to Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam.

Brahmi travelled far beyond India too. Scripts in [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], Myanmar, [[@thailand|Thailand]], Cambodia and Tibet all grew from it, carried by traders, monks and Buddhist texts. A Thai or Tibetan letter can be a distant cousin of a Hindi one.

If the letters share an ancestor, why do they look so unlike each other? [[@writing-tools|Writing tools]] played a part. In the south, people wrote for centuries on dried palm leaves, scratching letters with an iron stylus. One popular explanation is that long straight lines would split the leaf along its [[vein|veins]], so southern scripts grew round and curly, as you can see in Malayalam, Telugu and Kannada.

In the north, many scribes wrote with ink and a reed pen. Devanagari gained its long top line, the *shirorekha*, from which letters seem to hang like clothes on a washing line. Bengali and Gurmukhi have top lines too. Telugu and Kannada scripts are so alike that a reader of one can often guess at words in the other.

By the 1700s, nobody could read Brahmi. The [[inscription|inscriptions]] on Ashoka's pillars were a mystery. In 1837, James Prinsep, an Englishman working at the mint in Kolkata, cracked the code. He noticed that many short inscriptions on a [[stupa|stupa]] at Sanchi ended with the same two letters. He guessed they recorded gifts and that the letters spelled *danam*, "gift". He was right, and the rest of the script followed.

The even older script of the Indus cities, used more than 4,000 years ago, has never been deciphered. Its inscriptions are very short, mostly on small seals, and no bilingual text like Egypt's [[@hieroglyphs|Rosetta Stone]] has been found. Some scholars even doubt it wrote down a full language. The story of India's scripts still has a missing first chapter.

text: [[@food-why-bananas-curve|केले टेढ़े इसलिए होते हैं]] क्योंकि बढ़ते समय वे अपनी दिशा बदलते हैं। केले का गुच्छा एक भारी डंठल से लटकता है जो नीचे की ओर झुकी रहती है, इसलिए शुरू में छोटे-छोटे फलों का मुँह ज़मीन की तरफ़ होता है।

फिर कुछ मज़ेदार होता है। हर केला [[gravity|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] से दूर और धूप की ओर बढ़ने लगता है, और ऊपर की तरफ़ मुड़ जाता है। वनस्पति वैज्ञानिक इसे नेगेटिव जियोट्रॉपिज़्म (ऋणात्मक गुरुत्वानुवर्तन) कहते हैं, यानी धरती के खिंचाव के उल्टा बढ़ना। केले का नीचे वाला हिस्सा ऊपर वाले हिस्से से तेज़ बढ़ता है, इसलिए फल मुड़कर अपना जाना-पहचाना आकार ले लेता है।

sec.t:
केले का पौधा दो मंज़िला मकान से भी ऊँचा हो सकता है, पर उसमें लकड़ी नहीं होती। जो तना दिखता है, उसे स्यूडोस्टेम, यानी “नकली तना” कहते हैं। यह बड़े-बड़े पत्तों के निचले हिस्सों से बना होता है, जो अख़बार की तरह एक-दूसरे पर कसकर लिपटे रहते हैं।

असली तना ज़मीन के नीचे रहता है। जब पौधा एक गुच्छा दे देता है, तो उसका नकली तना सूख जाता है और काट दिया जाता है। उसकी जड़ के पास से नए अंकुर निकलते हैं, जिन्हें सकर कहते हैं, और यही आगे बढ़ते हैं। किसान बीज की जगह यही अंकुर लगाते हैं। एक गुच्छे में सौ से भी कहीं ज़्यादा केले हो सकते हैं। ये कतारों में लगे होते हैं, जिन्हें अंग्रेज़ी में “हैंड” यानी हाथ कहते हैं, और हर केला एक “फ़िंगर” यानी उँगली कहलाता है।

जंगली केले सख़्त काले बीजों से भरे होते हैं, जो काली मिर्च के दानों जितने बड़े होते हैं, और उनमें गूदा बहुत कम होता है। हज़ारों साल पहले न्यू गिनी और दक्षिण-पूर्व एशिया के किसानों को कुछ ऐसे दुर्लभ पौधे मिले जिनमें लगभग बीज ही नहीं थे। उन्होंने अंकुर लगा-लगाकर इन पौधों को फैलाया।

इसलिए दुकान में मिलने वाले केले क्लोन हैं, यानी ऐसे पौधे जो आनुवंशिक रूप से लगभग एक जैसे हैं। इससे उन्हें उगाना आसान हो जाता है, पर खतरा भी रहता है। 1950 के दशक में पनामा रोग नाम की एक मिट्टी वाली [[fungus|फफूँद]] ने ग्रॉस मिशेल केले के ज़्यादातर बागान तबाह कर दिए। उस समय विदेश भेजे जाने वाले केलों में यही दुनिया की सबसे पसंदीदा किस्म थी। उगाने वालों ने कैवेंडिश अपना लिया। अब उसी रोग का एक नया रूप एशिया, अफ़्रीका और लैटिन अमेरिका में कैवेंडिश के खेतों पर हमला कर रहा है।

भारत किसी भी और देश से ज़्यादा केले उगाता है, दुनिया की कुल फ़सल का लगभग एक-चौथाई। इनमें से ज़्यादातर भारत में ही खा लिए जाते हैं। यहाँ दर्जनों देसी किस्में हैं: छोटा, मीठा इलायची केला, लाल केला, और [[@kerala|केरल]] का बड़ा नेंद्रन, जिसे तलकर केले के चिप्स बनते हैं।

पौधे का लगभग हर हिस्सा काम आता है। कच्चे केले की सब्ज़ी बनती है, बैंगनी फूल से एक अलग पकवान बनता है, और तने का भीतरी गूदा भी पकाया जाता है। केले के पत्ते थाली का काम करते हैं, खासकर [[@south-indian-meals|त्योहारों की दावतों]] में, जैसे ओणम की दावत। इसके बारे में तुम [[@onam-pongal|ओणम और पोंगल]] में पढ़ सकते हो।

केले में पोटैशियम भरपूर होता है, एक ऐसा [[mineral|खनिज]] जिसकी ज़रूरत तुम्हारी नसों और मांसपेशियों को होती है। कुदरती पोटैशियम का एक बहुत छोटा-सा हिस्सा [[radioactive|रेडियोधर्मी]] रूप में होता है, इसलिए केले भी ज़रा-से रेडियोधर्मी होते हैं। और इसी वजह से तुम भी।

यह मात्रा इतनी कम है कि किसी को कोई नुकसान नहीं पहुँचा सकती। वैज्ञानिक कभी-कभी मज़ाक में “बनाना इक्विवैलेंट डोज़”, यानी “एक केले जितनी खुराक” की बात करते हैं, ताकि समझा सकें कि रोज़मर्रा का विकिरण कितना कम होता है।
